title: Lift Up Your Eyes and Look in Every Direction — Separating, Choosing, Seeing
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. Last lesson we watched a man of seventy-five set out on the strength of a single sentence — and we also watched him, not long after that call, go down into Egypt, tell a lie to save his own skin, and finally be escorted out by Pharaoh with his face in the dust.

In today's lesson we are going to watch him walk back out of that humiliating place. And along the way there will be a family conflict — very possibly the very kind of conflict you are facing this week.
So let me put a question to you first. When you find yourself in a conflict with someone, and you are plainly in the right — what do you do?

Let me put the answer up front: yielding is not weakness. A person yields because he knows his portion is not held in anybody's hand. Lot lifted up his eyes and saw good land for himself; Abram lifted up his eyes only after God told him to raise his head.
1. After a Fall, Walk Back to the Beginning
Verse 1: "Abram went up out of Egypt—he, his wife, all that he had, and Lot with him—into the South."

Brothers and sisters, notice that verb: "went up", וַיַּעַל (*vaya'al*). Verse 10 of the last chapter said he "went down into Egypt", וַיֵּרֶד (*vayered*). The same pair of direction words — one down, one up. The road he went down by, he is now walking back up, the very way he came.

Verse 3 puts it even more carefully: "He went on his journeys from the South as far as Bethel, to the place where his tent had been at the beginning, between Bethel and Ai, to the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first."

"He went on his journeys" is in Hebrew לְמַסָּעָיו (*lemasa'av*), literally "according to his pullings-up of camp" — one encampment after another. Which is to say: he did not take a shortcut straight back. He retraced the route by which he had first come out, stage by stage, camp by camp, all the way home.

Then verse 4: "There Abram called on Yahweh's name." Brothers and sisters, that sentence is word for word what Genesis 12:8 had already said of him. He goes back to the place where the line was cut, and joins it up again.

This passage gives us an intensely practical lesson: after a fall, the right direction is not forward at a run — it is back to the beginning. A great many people, once they have failed, react by working twice as hard, changing their surroundings, throwing themselves into some new piece of service, as though doing a little more might cover the thing over. But the Bible's method is not to charge forward. It is to walk back — back to the days when you were still all right, back to the last place where you and God talked properly.

Revelation 2:5 — the Lord Jesus says to the church in Ephesus, "Remember therefore from where you have fallen, and repent and do the first works." The same direction exactly. Look back, and then do again what you did at the first.
"Back to the place of the altar he had made at the first" — after a fall, must I really go back to the beginning? Can I not simply start again from where I am now?

You can start from where you are now, so long as you are clear about what "the beginning" means. Genesis 13:4 says he came back "to the place of the altar, which he had made there at the first. There Abram called on Yahweh's name" — and that is not superstition about a spot on a map. It is a return to the state in which his relationship with God was at its clearest. So in practice this is not about going back to a particular church or a particular conference. It is about going back to the things you were doing then and have since stopped doing: reading the Bible, praying, meeting with God's people, that fixed stretch of quiet. When a person drifts, what usually goes first is those few small things. Going back to the beginning simply means starting those few small things again — and you do not have to wait until your mood improves before you begin.
2. The Land Was Not Able to Bear Them

Verses 5 and 6: "Lot also, who went with Abram, had flocks, herds, and tents. The land was not able to bear them, that they might live together; for their possessions were so great that they couldn't live together."
The word behind "was not able to bear" is נָשָׂא (*nasa*), which means to lift, to carry, to hold a weight up. The land could not carry the two households.

Brothers and sisters, here is something well worth noticing: the cause of the quarrel was not poverty. It was prosperity. Verse 2 says Abram "was very rich in livestock, in silver, and in gold", and the Hebrew there is כָּבֵד מְאֹד (*kaved me'od*), literally "very heavy" — and that root is the same root as the word for glory, כָּבוֹד (*kavod*).

So the text is making a rather beautiful pun: the man was heavy. The blessing had grown until it became a weight, until two families could no longer fit into the same place. I have seen it far too often in pastoral work — the fiercest quarrel in a family is very often not in its poorest season, but in the season when there is finally something to divide.

Verse 7: "The Canaanites and the Perizzites lived in the land at that time." Brothers and sisters, why does the author drop that sentence in just here? What has it got to do with two sets of herdsmen quarrelling?

It has everything to do with it. That sentence is the camera swinging round to remind you: there are other people standing nearby, and they are watching. A quarrel inside God's household has never once been a matter behind closed doors. And the very first reason Abram gives in his next breath is exactly that: "Please, let there be no strife between you and me… for we are relatives."

In verse 8 the phrase "let there be no strife" is in Hebrew אַל־נָא תְהִי מְרִיבָה (*al-na tehi merivah*). That אַל־נָא is the gentlest form of dissuasion the language has — not a command, a plea. Brothers and sisters, he is the elder here. He could have given an order. What he chose was, "please, let there not be."
"The land was not able to bear them" — is it normal for blessing to bring conflict instead?

Entirely normal, and the text says so in the plainest words: "for their possessions were so great that they couldn't live together." A great many relationships do not break under scarcity; they break under abundance. When there is not enough, people need each other. When there is plenty, people begin to argue over where the boundary runs. This holds for a clan, for a church, for a team of co-workers alike: the giving goes up, the ministry grows larger, the resources increase — and the tension surfaces. So what has to be handled in advance is not the resources; it is the rules — who decides, how things get divided, how a disagreement gets talked through. Abram's method was to speak up before the quarrel could spread: "Please, let there be no strife between you and me… for we are relatives." He talks about the relationship first, and only then about dividing the land.
Abram was the elder, and yet he let Lot choose first. Was that not simply weakness?

We have to tell yielding and weakness apart. Weakness is not daring to face a thing and pushing the problem further down the road. Abram took the initiative: he proposed the solution himself, and then he handed the right of choice over. That is something only a person with strength can do — and the reason he dared to yield is that he knew the land was not Lot's to give. It was God's. So the real question is not "ought I to yield or not?" but "when you yield, who are you leaning on inside?" If you give way and are then full of grievance, telling everyone who will listen about it, that is not yielding. It is suppression. Here is the practical test: after you have given way, can you pray for the good of the other person? If you can, it was faith. If you cannot, deal with your own heart first and talk about the matter afterwards.
3. A Light from the Original: Two Liftings of the Eyes
Verse 9: "Isn't the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left."

Brothers and sisters, think carefully about what Abram is giving up here. First, he is the elder and Lot is his nephew; in that culture, the elder choosing first was simply the order of things. Second, this land had been promised to him — in Genesis 12:7 God said with his own mouth, "I will give this land to your offspring." Third, Abram is the one who brought Lot out in the first place; everything Lot owns has, to some degree, come to him through his uncle.
By seniority, by promise, by length of standing — on every count he was the one who should have picked first. And what he says is: you choose.
What comes next is the decisive contrast of the whole chapter, and it is hidden inside two liftings of the eyes.
Verse 10: "Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere… like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar."

Notice that the author has packed two place names into one sentence. "The garden of Yahweh" — that is Eden. "The land of Egypt" — that is the place they have only just scrambled out of in disgrace. Brothers and sisters, it looks like paradise, and it is in fact the road back. And the text immediately slips in one more clause: "before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah." The reader is told how this ends before the choice has even been made.
Verse 11: "So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one another." East again. That is the fifth time in Genesis.

Then verse 12 carries a sentence that lands very lightly and is absolutely lethal: "Lot lived in the cities of the plain, and moved his tent as far as Sodom." Moved his tent — by degrees. Brothers and sisters, nobody walks into Sodom in a single stride. On the day he shifted the tent, Lot would not have felt that he was sinning. By Genesis 14:12 the text simply says of him that he "lived in Sodom." By Genesis 19:1 he is sitting in the gate of the city — and the gate is where the elders sit. Between "moved his tent" and "sitting in the gate" there is not one obvious moment of falling anywhere to be found.
And then verse 14: "Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, 'Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward.'"

The same action, two different subjects. Lot lifted up his own eyes and saw a well-watered plain. Abram was told by God to lift up his eyes, and then God said, "for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever."

Brothers and sisters, the man who gave it away is the one who ends up seeing more. And notice the timing — God speaks these words only after Lot has already gone. At the moment you yield, you cannot see this paragraph at all. All you know in that moment is that you have lost out.
Lot "lifted up his eyes" and chose the fertile plain. What exactly was wrong with choosing that?

There is nothing wrong with choosing good land in itself, and the text nowhere says that Lot sinned. The problem lies in what he saw and in what he did not see. Verse 10 says he saw "all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere… as you go to Zoar" — but in that very same verse the author has slipped in the words "before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah", and verse 13 adds, "Now the men of Sodom were exceedingly wicked and sinners against Yahweh." In other words, he saw the terms of the land; he did not see the air of the place. That is intensely practical for us when we are choosing a school, a job, a place to live: look at the terms, certainly — but look harder at what that environment will make of you. You become the kind of person you breathe in every day.
Lot lifting up his eyes and Abram lifting up his eyes are the same action. Where does the difference lie?

The difference lies in who told him to lift them. In verse 10 it is Lot himself who "lifted up his eyes, and saw". In verse 14 it is "Yahweh said to Abram… 'Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward.'" One man picked out for himself what looked good; the other was told by God to look. And the timing is fascinating — God does not say this until Lot has already left. There are two things in that for us. First: whatever has been taken out of your hands, God will show you something larger. Second: the best seeing very often happens after the letting go. So when you are facing a choice, there is one thing you may ask for — Lord, do not let me see only what I want to see. You lift my eyes.
4. The Promised Land and One Burial Cave
Verses 16 and 17: "I will make your offspring as the dust of the earth… Arise, walk through the land in its length and in its width; for I will give it to you."

"Walk through the land in its length and in its width" was a legal act in the ancient Near East — to walk over a piece of ground was the way a man declared his title to it. God is telling him to go and walk it.

But brothers and sisters, I want to say something very honest at this point. In the whole of his life, the only thing Abraham actually owned in that land was a burial cave. Genesis 23 records that he paid four hundred shekels of silver to the Hittites for the cave of Machpelah, in order to bury Sarah. God said he would give him the entire land. All he ever bought in it was one grave.

And Hebrews 11:13 says, "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

So the promise in this chapter is not a cheque you can cash today. It is a direction — a direction that will take several hundred years to walk. This has to be said plainly, or we will raise a congregation of believers who expect to be rich by tomorrow, and whose faith will not survive the first month in which nothing is delivered.
Verse 18, the close of the whole chapter: "Abram moved his tent, and came and lived by the oaks of Mamre, which are in Hebron, and built an altar there to Yahweh."

Brothers and sisters, look at how this chapter is built. Up out of Egypt; back to the place of the altar he had made at the first, and there he calls on the name of God — then a family conflict is handled — then he moves to the place God points him to — and then he builds another altar. An altar at the head, an altar at the tail. The conflict in the middle is held between two altars.
God promised to give Abram the land, and yet all he ever bought was a single burial cave. Does that count as the promise being kept?

Hebrews 11 gives us the answer. These people "all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar", and it goes on to say that "they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one." So the fulfilment did not come in his generation — and he lived his whole life according to the promise all the same. That burial cave matters enormously: it is a stake driven into the promised land, the proof that he believed this ground would one day belong to his offspring. That is very practical for us. You may well not see, in this lifetime, the completion of the thing you have been asking for. But you can do something like buying a burial cave — one concrete act, pointing at a future you will not live to see, which proves that you really do believe.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "yielding" as though it meant that you may never contend about anything at any time. In the very next chapter, Abram leads out three hundred and eighteen men and pursues an army for hundreds of kilometres in order to rescue Lot; in chapter 21 he confronts Abimelech to his face over a well of water. So the biblical principle is not "give way in everything." It is: over possessions you may give way, and over justice you must speak. Fail to make that distinction and we will raise a congregation of people who dare not face a problem and who have learned to call their avoidance humility — and that does damage to families and to churches alike.

The second is preaching Lot as a villain. 2 Peter 2:7 calls him "righteous Lot", and says that he was "very distressed by the lustful life of the wicked." His problem was not his nature; it was the direction of his choosing. Demonise him and your congregation will never see the same tendency in themselves — and that tendency is in every last one of us.

The third is taking "I will give all the land which you see to you" and preaching it as: believe in the Lord and you will get rich. The promise of verse 15 concerns offspring and the plan of God; it is not a guarantee of personal wealth. And let us be honest about it: the man who received this promise managed, in the course of his whole life, to buy exactly one cave in that land.

The fourth is preaching the parting of the two households and never reaching the altar. That altar in verse 18 is the close of the whole chapter. If all you preach is technique for handling people — how to communicate, how to concede, how to defuse a conflict — then this chapter has turned into a class in communication skills. The real point of this chapter is not that Abram was good with people. It is that he knew the one dividing up the land was not Lot.

The fifth is turning "traveled east" into a mechanical rule, as though heading east on the map were itself a sin. This is a literary sense of direction, not a navigation instruction. The author uses it to mark the flavour of departure. Preach it as a literal rule of geography and your congregation will start worrying about which way their next house faces — and that is putting the last thing first.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: the two things most likely to blow a Chinese family apart are the dividing of the family property and the sharing out of the duty to care for ageing parents. Can this chapter be applied to that directly? Brothers and sisters, it can — but it must be applied carefully. Here is where it applies: what Abram gave up was the very thing he had the right to take first, and he dared to give it up because he knew that the one who divides the land is God. For a family currently deadlocked over an inheritance, that is an intensely practical reminder — the piece you are fighting for, can it really determine what your portion is going to be? And here is where care is needed: this chapter must never be used to demand of the person who has always been losing out that he should "give way one more time." In a great many Chinese families there is always one person who has been giving way all along — usually the one who does the most for the parents, or the one who is least able to speak up for himself. If you preach this chapter at him, you are simply helping the people who have always been taking. So be clear about it: this chapter is preached to the person who holds the right to choose first. It is not preached to the person who has been sacrificed all along.

The second question: I have kept giving way in order to avoid conflict, and the result is that my family have only become more unreasonable — how long exactly am I supposed to go on enduring? Brothers and sisters, on this one I want to give you three very concrete distinctions. First, distinguish between possessions and justice. What Abram gave up was pasture, not principle; the moment Lot was in danger he sent out his men, and when Abimelech's servants seized a well, he said so straight out. Second, distinguish between enduring and enabling. To endure is to choose not to fight for what is rightfully mine. To enable is to let a person go on hurting other people, or go on hurting himself. Third, distinguish who is being harmed. If I give way and the only one who loses is me, then I may give way. If I give way and the one harmed is my spouse, my child, or someone else weaker than I am, then that is not humility — that is dereliction of duty. And please remember this: when Abram gave way, he did it from a place of solid ground, and his ground was "God will give it to me." If your enduring comes out of fear, that is not the yielding this chapter is teaching. That is fear — and the thing that needs healing is the fear itself.
When a family has to divide up property and responsibilities, how do we keep it from turning into the strife of Genesis 13?

Four very practical principles. First, talk before the thing grows large; do not wait until the herdsmen are already fighting. Second, speak about the relationship before you speak about the terms — say "we are one family" first, and say it out loud. Third, the one who gives way needs solid ground under him: that ground is not shrewd calculation, it is knowing that your portion is in God's hands. Fourth, write the decisions down; do not leave them resting on the spoken word alone. Putting it in writing is not distrust, it is protecting the relationship. And one more thing that matters a great deal: after the division, do not cut off contact. Abram divided the land, and when Lot was carried off captive in chapter 14, he still took his men and went to rescue him. Separating is not the same thing as no longer being family.
7. Living 321 Out — My Portion Is Given by God
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Abram handed the better land to his nephew. And the Lord Jesus said, "even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many." Philippians 2 says of him that he "didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped." Brothers and sisters, my role model is perfectly clear: what he gave up was not a piece of ground, it was the glory of heaven. Set beside that, the piece I am fighting over today is really very small.

The Bible is my standard — and the standard in this chapter is not "how much did you give away" but "on what grounds did you give it away." Abram gave way because of that sentence God had spoken in Genesis 12:7. This is exactly what a standard is for: at the moment of conflict, it remembers on your behalf what God has said. A person whose impression of God's promises is vague will find it very hard to let go at the decisive moment.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — notice once more the difference between the two liftings of the eyes. Nobody told Lot to lift his; he looked on his own account. Abram lifted his because God said, "Now, lift up your eyes, and look." Brothers and sisters, it is the same act of looking, and yet one pair of eyes is being led by desire and the other is being pointed by God. The guidance of the Holy Spirit is very often precisely this: he decides what you see first.

Let Jesus be King — Lot lifted up his eyes first; Abram waited until God told him to lift his. One man chose for himself; the other was shown. To let Jesus be King is to hand over the sentence "which one am I going to pick" and let him say it instead. And the hardest thing about doing that is this: at the moment you hand it over, you cannot see a thing.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — this chapter ends at an altar. Abram did not put up a monument to his own graciousness; what he built was an altar to God. Brothers and sisters, the moment at which glory is most easily stolen from him is usually not the moment we fail. It is the moment we have just done something beautifully right.

Establish God's system — God says, "for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever." That is a promise of territory, and it is also the first outline of the kingdom of God. And what Abram does after receiving that promise is to move to Mamre and build an altar. To establish God's system is to build an altar on the piece of ground God has pointed us to — not to put up the city first, but to put up the altar first.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about selflessness, about denying of self, about not contending — and all of that is right, and this chapter gives us a beautiful demonstration of it. But please, always preach the other half alongside it: in chapter 14 Abram takes up arms to rescue a man, and in chapter 21 he speaks up over a well. If we preach only the giving way and never say when a person ought to stand up, then "selflessness" becomes the most convenient sentence in the church — convenient for telling other people to be quiet. Real selflessness is "I will not fight for myself." It is not "I will not speak for what is just."
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Lifting of the Eyes
Brothers and sisters, the same act of lifting up the eyes falls into four different kinds of heart, and what each of them sees is completely different.

The proud heart lifts up its eyes and sees how handsomely it gave way. This is the heart that afterwards tells a great many people, "You know, I could easily have chosen first." Brothers and sisters, what Abram did after he gave way was to move his tent and build an altar; the text does not record a single line of his feelings about it. Real yielding has no need of an audience.

The fearful heart lifts up its eyes and sees, "If I give this away, I will have nothing left." This heart is not unwilling to yield; it does not dare to. To that heart I want to say: look at the timing. God did not say "lift up your eyes, and look" until Lot had already gone. Which means that at the moment you give way, you genuinely cannot see the compensation — and that is exactly where faith is really tested. And Matthew 6:33 says, "But seek first God's Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well."

The ashamed heart lifts up its eyes and sees, "It was never going to be my turn to choose anyway." At home and in church, this heart has always been the one who gets arranged around, and after long enough it stops believing that it has any right of choice at all. Brothers and sisters, let me say this very carefully: this chapter is not a rebuke aimed at you. It is aimed at the person who holds the right to choose first. What God says to you is that sentence in verse 14 — he goes in person to a man who has been left behind, tells him to raise his head, and says: look, all of this is going to be yours.

The wounded heart lifts up its eyes and sees the person who has always been taking. You may have been giving way for twenty years, and the other party has not once turned round. Brothers and sisters, I am not going to tell you that one more concession will put it right. What I want to tell you is the timing of verse 14: God did not open his mouth until Lot had gone. He did not step into the middle of the quarrel to take Abram's side. He waited until the dust had settled, and then he spoke to him himself. God has seen everything you have swallowed. It is only that the timing of his speaking is very often later than we would like.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, find your own "place of the altar which you made at the first." Think back to a season when your relationship with God was at its best — what were you doing then, at what hour did you read the Bible, who were you walking alongside? This week, restore one of those things. After a fall, the direction is backwards.

Second, give way once, deliberately, in something small. A parking space, the order of speaking, who takes first, whose opinion gets adopted. Give way once on purpose — and tell nobody at all that you did.

Third, work out which kind of enduring yours is. Write down one thing you are currently putting up with, and then ask three questions. Is what I am giving up a possession, or a principle? Is my enduring allowing someone weaker than me to be harmed? And is the engine of my yielding faith, or is it fear?

Fourth, keep an eye on your own "by degrees." Lot moved his tent a little at a time. This week, examine one thing you are slowly drifting towards without feeling there is anything wrong with it — a relationship, a habit, a pattern of spending, a website.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences: there is a man in the Bible, an uncle, and the land had been promised to him by God — and he let his nephew choose first, and the nephew walked off with the best of it; only after that nephew had gone did God tell him to raise his head and say, "I will give all the land which you see to you"; so here is the thing I learned — the person who dares to give way is not doing it because he does not care, but because he knows the one who divides things up is not the man standing opposite him.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my portion is given to me by God, and so I do not have to snatch it out of anybody's hand.
I declare that I will give way over possessions and speak up for justice; humility is not avoidance.
I declare that I will not choose by what my own eyes can see; I will wait until he tells me to lift them.
I declare that after a fall I will walk back to the beginning, and not charge forward in order to cover the failure over.
This week I am supposed to "give way once" — but I have given way many times already, and the other person simply keeps pushing further. What do I do?

Yielding is not the absence of boundaries. What Abram gave up was land, not principle; he handed over the right of choice and still kept his own tent, his own people, his own altar. So be clear about the line: what may be given away is advantage, precedence and face. What may not be given away is truth, safety, and your relationship with God. If in a relationship you are the one giving every single time and the other person is the one taking every single time, that is not humility — it is an imbalance, and somebody needs to state the boundary plainly. In practice: write down "what I can give way on, and what I cannot give way on", and go through the list with a spiritual companion. And if that relationship already involves verbal or physical harm, please seek out both pastoral and professional help, and do not carry it alone.
Brothers and sisters, if only one contrast from this lesson may remain, let it be the picture of two men raising their heads.

Lot raised his head, and what he saw was water and pasture, well-watered ground, a plain that looked like Eden and looked like Egypt. He chose it, and then he travelled east, moving his tent by degrees until he reached Sodom. By chapter 19 he is being dragged out of that city by angels, and he has lost his wife, lost his estate, and lost the respect of his children.

Abram raised his head because God told him to raise it. And what God gave him was not the piece lying in front of his eyes: it was "northward and southward and eastward and westward", it was "forever", it was "your offspring as the dust of the earth."
The same action, two different endings. And the difference does not lie in which man had the better eye. It lies in who it was that told him to raise his head.

And I want you to notice one last thing. The piece of land Abram gave away was later burned to scorched earth by sulphur and fire; while the place he moved to — Hebron, which looked like the poorer option — became the home of his whole life, and the ground in which he was finally buried. The choice that looked at the time like losing out did not show its worth for another forty years.
Brothers and sisters, the one who gives way is not the loser. He has simply not yet come to the day of reckoning.

The focus is not on how much I gave away, not on what the other person took, and not on whether anybody noticed what I have swallowed. The focus is on Jesus — what he gave up was the glory of heaven, and God highly exalted him. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: to dare to give way in one thing, and then, in the very place where we gave way, to build an altar. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at the level of mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★ After a fall, "going back to the place of the altar he had made at the first" — what does that concretely mean today?
2. ★★★ Lot lifted up his eyes on his own account; Abram lifted his because God told him to. In your own decisions, what is the difference between those two kinds of looking?
3. ★ "The land was not able to bear them" — why is it that so many relationships break down not in scarcity but in abundance?
4. ★★ In his whole life Abram bought only one burial cave. How does that help us understand a promise we have not yet seen fulfilled?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (when I give way, it shows how generous I am), fearful (if I give it away I will have nothing left), ashamed (I dare not fight for anything, and I dare not speak), wounded (I have given way so many times and nobody remembers). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ The last choice you made — did you look first at the terms on offer, or first at what that environment would make of you?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing I am least willing to give away is …"
9. ★★ This week, in which one matter will you give way? Say clearly whether what you are giving up is an advantage or a principle.

Leader's reminder: question eleven will touch the grievance of someone who has been taken advantage of for a long time. If somebody speaks about an unbalanced relationship, first affirm what he has given, and do not rush to urge him to go on enduring; if harm is involved, follow up with him privately after the meeting and help him find the support he needs.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.

10. ★★ In your own family, is there a matter of property, of responsibility or of arrangement that ought to be talked about early rather than left until a quarrel starts? Say how you will open the conversation.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: in your workplace or your ministry team, which rule ought to be spelled out clearly now?
12. ★★★ The back-to-the-beginning practice: this week, restart one small spiritual habit you used to have and later let drop. Say which one it is, and in what time slot you will do it.

13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the matter in which you are going to give way, and ask him to ask you on the seventh day how it went. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First, in the Bible two households had to part because there was too much between them. Second, the elder handed the right of first choice to the younger man, because he knew his own portion was not given to him by people. Third, so here is what I learned: the person who dares to give way is a person with solid ground under his heart. Write down now who you will tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the matter in which you will give way this week, and the one small habit you are going to restart. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord that when we make our choices we would first lift up our eyes and look in the direction he points.
